newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SBC confident of smooth Dillon integration.
newsitem.headline: SBC confident of smooth Dillon integration.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) on Thursday announced a $600 million deal to buy Wall Street investment bank Dillon, Read & Co and said it was confident that integration of the U.S. firm would go smoothly without major layoffs.

"We don't expect any problems whatsoever...there aren't any overlaps," SBC chief executive Marcel Ospel told Reuters in a telephone interview, adding, "There aren't any negative synergies at all which would lead to a reduction of staff."

SBC, in stepping into the gap left by Dutch financial services ING Groep NV, said the agreement called for the merger of Dillon Read with its existing investment banking arm SBC Warburg to form SBC Warburg Dillon Read.
The deal requires U.S. Federal Reserve Board and other regulatory approvals.
SBC will finance the move into corporate finance and advisory work in the U.S. with existing shares and said it would not result in a material dilution of earnings.

Analysts said the bank was paying around three times book value for the management-owned firm, underlining the high prices currently being commanded for a slice of U.S. corporate advisory work and securities business.
Ospel said the price was more than justified given the benefits gained.

"Dillon Read will have more access to capital and a much larger product base and our clients in Europe, Far Eastern and emerging market clients will have U.S. product opportunities in in M&A advise with execution capability which will only enhance the (client) relationships in both regions," Ospel said.
In addition, he said SBC Warburg intended to apply schemes similar to those used to keep key management in past acquisitions.
One source familiar with the talks said the arrangement called for staggered payments over a 2-1/2 year period for the shares of Dillon Read's top people.
Ospel said Dillon Read chief executive Franklin Hobbs will assume the role of head of corporate finance for SBC Warburg Dillon Read out of London.

Dillon Read, which was founded in 1832, employs 730 people and has offices in New York, Boston, San Francisco, Dallas, London, Paris and Tokyo. It is 75 percent owned by its management, with the remainder held by ING Barings.

Plans by the Dutch group ING to strengthen its own position on Wall Street collapsed on Wednesday when talks on buying out the Dillon Read management ended. Reports that SBC was interested only emerged overnight after the announcement.
Banking sources said the deal had been struck quickly, although Dillon Read was widely believed to be in talks with other parties while negotiating with ING.
Ospel said the talks with Dillon had been going on for about two months.

The Dillon Read partners had an option to buy ING's 25 percent stake which ING had said it expected them to exercise when talks ended. The partners are believed to have the right to buy the stake back at book value, which put them in a strong position to negotiate with other parties.
SBC Warburg, was established when SBC took over British merchant bank SG Warburg. The firm is based in London and employs around 9,000 people in 40 countries, 2,000 of them in the U.S.
Analysts said that while the cost of Dillon Read was high, the crucial element of the deal would be the clauses dictating how key personnel would fit in within the new group.
The relationship nature of Dillon Read's business will make it especially important that partners are locked into the merged entity, therefore keeping the firm's existing client base.
"The key relationships are going to make or break the deal," John Leonard, banking analyst at Salomon Brothers, told Reuters.
Last year, Dillon Read advised on 50 mergers and acquisitions totalling $45 billion. It is also active in the high yield, equity and private placement markets.
SBC said Dillon Read had completed deals worth more than $8.0 billion in these markets in 1996.
Leonard said the deal "made a lot of sense" from a strategic point of view as it gave SBC the good addition of a largely U.S. oriented corporate finance and investment banking house.

For Dillon Read the deal not only means a windfall for the partners, but also the guarantee of not being turned into a niche mergers and acquisitions player without the capitalisation needed to compete with the first tier players.

"The combination is an excellent fit for both firms, as it will enhance significantly the capabilities and resources we are able to offer our clients," Dillon Read president Franklin Hobbs said in a statement.
